choices.title: Wound dehiscence
choices.correct_explanation:
• Wound dehiscence is defined as the partial or complete separation of the surgical incision edges without protrusion of internal organs. In contrast, Evisceration involves separation of the wound with extrusion of internal organs, making it a more severe condition.
  • Abscess formation refers to a localized collection of pus, while a hematoma is a collection of blood within tissues; neither presents with separation of wound edges.
  • Clinically, wound dehiscence most commonly occurs around the 5th to 7th postoperative day, often associated with factors such as infection, poor wound healing, malnutrition, or increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., coughing).

Table: Wound dehiscence

Aspect

Details

Definition

Partial or complete separation of a surgical wound along sutured layers.

Types

·         Superficial: Involves skin and subcutaneous tissue.

·         Deep: Involves fascia and muscle layers (risk of evisceration).

Risk Factors

·         Patient-related: Malnutrition, obesity, smoking, diabetes, immunosuppression.

·         Surgical-related: Inadequate closure, tension on sutures, infection, emergency surgery.

Clinical Features

·         Sudden discharge of serosanguinous fluid.

·         Visible separation of wound edges.

·         Possible protrusion of underlying tissues (e.g., evisceration in severe cases).

Prevention

·         Adequate pre-op nutrition and glycemic control.

·         Use of tension-free sutures and proper technique.

·         Avoiding excessive strain on the wound (e.g., coughing, lifting).

·         Prompt treatment of infections.

Management

·         Minor (Superficial): Regular dressing, wound care, antibiotics if infection is present.

·         Major (Deep): Surgical re-closure under sterile conditions.

·         Evisceration: Cover exposed tissues with saline-soaked sterile gauze; urgent surgery.

Complications

Infection, delayed healing, hernia formation, recurrence of dehiscence.

choices.title: Measure from nose → ear → xiphoid process
choices.correct_explanation:
• Before inserting a nasogastric (NG) tube, it is essential to estimate the correct insertion length to ensure that the tube reaches the stomach rather than remaining in the esophagus or inadvertently entering the airway.
  • The standard method used for this purpose is the NEX method, which stands for Nose → Ear → Xiphoid process. In this method, the distance from the nose to the ear (N–E) represents the length from the nostril to the oropharynx, while the distance from the ear to the xiphoid process (E–X) corresponds to the path from the pharynx through the esophagus to the stomach.
  • The sum of these measurements provides an approximate length that the NG tube must be inserted to reach the stomach safely and effectively.

    Ryle’s tube/ Nasogastric (NG) tube

  • Ryle’s tube (RT), also known as nasogastric (NG) tube, measures 120-125 cm.
  • It has 4 markings at 40 cm (cardia), 50 cm (body), 60 cm (pylorus), and 70 cm (duodenum) to indicate the approximate position after the placement.
  • Indications for NG tube
    • Feeding in patients with dysphagia, decreased appetite, or those who are nil per os (NPO) for medical or surgical reasons.
    • Aspiration of gastric fluid.
    • Gastric decompression in cases of intestinal obstruction and paralytic ileus.
    • Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
    • Bowel irrigation.
  • The absolute contraindications for an NG tube are severe midface trauma, recent nasal surgery, and basilar skull fractures.
  • Steps for the correct insertion of RT in an adult:

    i. Examination of the patient’s nostril for any anatomical abnormalities and then instillation with 10 mL of 1% lignocaine.

    ii. NEX method is used to measure the length of the RT: Place the exit port of the tube at the tip of the nose. Extend the tube to the earlobe, and then to the xiphisternum.

    iii. The patient is asked to sit upright with partial neck flexion. The tip of the Ryle’s tube is lubricated and passed along the floor of the nasal passage until a resistance is felt (corresponds to nasopharynx).

    iv. The patient is subsequently asked to swallow water to guide the tube through the esophagus into the stomach until the marked length (based on the NEX method).

    v. NG tube is finally taped to secure it in place.

  • Confirmation of the correct position is done by:

    i. Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air.

    ii. X-ray chest to locate the lead markers.

    iii. Aspiration of contents and subsequently confirming gastric origin (pH <6 indicates gastric placement).

    Point to Remember:

  • The best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of Ryle’s tube (RT) is sitting with neck flexion. The described position helps in directing the RT towards the esophagus and also prevents it from coiling in the oropharynx or entering the trachea.
  • Selecting the length to be inserted in an adult and children:
    • NEX method (in adults) – Nose to ear to xiphisternum (Nose to around ear lobe and to umbilicus).
    • NEMU (preferred in children) – Nose to ear lobe to midpoint between xiphoid and umbilicus.

choices.title: Shock Index
choices.correct_explanation:
Shock Index (SI) is a rapid, bedside clinical tool widely used in emergency medicine and critical care to assess a patient’s hemodynamic stability. It helps in the early identification of shock, often before obvious hypotension develops.

Shock Index (SI) = Heart Rate (HR) / Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP)

Normal and Abnormal Values

  • Normal SI: 0.5 – 0.7
  • SI ≥ 0.9: Suggests early hemodynamic compromise
  • SI ≥ 1.0: Indicates significant shock, requiring urgent evaluation and intervention

Shock Index integrates two vital parameters:

  • Heart Rate (HR): rises in response to stress, hypovolemia, or shock
  • Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP): falls as circulatory failure progresses

A rising SI reflects a disproportionate increase in HR relative to SBP, which is often an early marker of circulatory collapse.

In Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), cyanotic (tet) spells occur due to increased right-to-left shunting across the ventricular septal defect, resulting in reduced pulmonary blood flow and worsening hypoxia.   

Squatting produces important hemodynamic changes:

·         Compression of lower limb veins → shifts blood to the central circulation → ↑ venous return (preload)  

·         Kinking of femoral arteries → ↑ systemic vascular resistance (SVR)

·         Improves right ventricular filling

choices.title: Speak calmly and set limits
choices.correct_explanation:
In psychiatric nursing, the principle of the “Least Restrictive Environment” is paramount. When a patient is aggressive or restless but not yet physically violent, the first line of intervention is always verbal de-escalation.

  • Speaking Calmly: Uses a “low and slow” voice to avoid mirroring. If nurse becomes excited or loud, patient’s agitation often increases.
  • Setting Limits: Clearly and firmly communicates which behaviors are unacceptable and what the consequences will be, providing the patient with a sense of structure and external control.
  • Pacing (Walking continuously): This is a physical manifestation of anxiety or psychomotor agitation. Allowing the patient to walk in a safe, supervised area can actually help them expend energy and reduce tension, provided they aren’t infringing on others’ space.

    Hierarchy of Restrictive Interventions

    They should be applied from least to most restrictive:

  • Verbal Intervention: De-escalation, active listening, and setting limits.
  • Chemical Intervention (PRN Medications): Offering oral medications (like Lorazepam) to help the patient calm down voluntarily.
  • Seclusion: Placing the patient in a safe, monitored room alone.
  • Physical/Chemical Restraints: Used only as a last resort when there is an immediate risk of harm to self or others.

    Other Options:

  • Option-B: Physical restraints are used only as a last resort when the patient poses an immediate danger to themselves or others.
  • Option-C: Chemical restraints are also considered a last resort and are used when de-escalation techniques fail.

choices.title: Imaginary exposure therapy
choices.correct_explanation:
In Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), patients often have intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions), like excessive washing. In this case:

  • The patient is asked to imagine touching dirty utensils (without actual exposure).
  • This is a form of exposure where the feared stimulus is presented mentally rather than physically.

In behavioral therapy, the method of confronting a feared object or situation is called “Exposure.” When this confrontation happens within the patient’s mind rather than in real life, it is termed Imaginary (or Imaginal) Exposure.

  • The Mechanism: For a patient with OCD, imagining the “dirty utensils” triggers the anxiety associated with the obsession (contamination).
  • The Goal: By repeatedly imagining the stimulus without performing the compulsion (dishwashing), the patient undergoes habituation, where the anxiety response gradually weakens over time.

    Other Options:

  • Option-a. Psychodynamic Therapy: This focuses on unconscious conflicts and childhood experiences rather than active behavioral modification for specific symptoms like dishwashing.
  • Option-c. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT): While used for OCD, ACT focuses on “psychological flexibility” and accepting thoughts rather than specifically using imagination to habituate to a trigger.

    Note: Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT) - While Imaginary Exposure is a component of CBT, it is a broad umbrella term.

  • Option B is the most specific and accurate description of the technique mentioned in the prompt.

    Obsessive Compulsive Disorder

  • Obsessive compulsive disorder is a disorder of thought possession.
  • Obsessive compulsive disorder is defined as the presence of obsessions and/or compulsions.
    • Obsessions are recurrent and persistent ideas, thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted and cause anxiety or distress to the patients.
    • Compulsions are the repetitive and intentional behaviors or acts performed in response to obsessions or according to certain rules that must be applied rigidly (e.g., repetitive hand washing, ritualistic checking).
  • The frequency of presenting patterns of OCD: Obsession of contamination > Pathological doubt > Intrusive thoughts > Symmetry.
  • In OCD, caudate nucleus part of the brain fails to act as the gatekeeper to allow the motor system to perform goal-directed activities.
  • Undoing, reaction formation, and isolation are the defence mechanisms involved in OCD.
  • In OCD, there is a decrease in the level of serotonin and an increase in the level of dopamine.
  • Treatment:
    • The treatment of choice for OCD is cognitive behavioral therapy, especially focusing on exposure and response prevention.
    • SSRI is the drug of choice in OCD. Clomipramine is the first FDA-approved agent for the treatment of OCD. In case of failure of 2 SSRIs, clomipramine is indicated.
    • Antipsychotics such as risperidone and aripiprazole can be used in SSRI-resistant cases to augment the response.

choices.correct_explanation:
• Nicotine gum should be used with the “chew and park” technique, where the patient chews the gum slowly until a peppery or tingling sensation appears, and then places (“parks”) it between the buccal mucosa and cheek to allow nicotine absorption through the oral mucosa (transmucosal absorption). This method enhances effectiveness and reduces side effects. If nicotine is swallowed, it undergoes first-pass metabolism in the liver, which significantly reduces its effectiveness and often leads to gastric irritation.

    The “Chew and Park” Technique:

    To ensure the patient receives the correct dose, the nurse must explain the following steps:

  • Chew: Bite the gum slowly until a “tingling” sensation or a peppery taste is felt.
  • Park: Stop chewing and “park” the gum between the cheek and the gumline. This is where the nicotine is absorbed into the bloodstream.
  • Repeat: Once the tingling sensation fades, chew again and park it in a different area of the mouth. This usually lasts about 30 minutes.

    Other Options:

  • Option-a. To Chew the gum fast: Chewing too quickly releases a “flood” of nicotine. This leads to common side effects like hiccups, sore throat, and nausea, as the nicotine is swallowed rather than absorbed.
  • Option-c. Swallow the saliva: While some swallowing is inevitable, patients should be encouraged to let the nicotine sit against the cheek. Excessive swallowing of nicotine-rich saliva causes dyspepsia (heartburn).
  • Option-d. Drink a cup of coffee: Acidic beverages (coffee, soda and juices) lower the pH of the mouth. Nicotine requires a more alkaline environment for optimal absorption; therefore, acidic drinks inhibit the effectiveness of gums. Patients should avoid these for 15 minutes before and during use.

False belief that a person's will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Exaggerated conception of one's importance, power, or identity.

False belief that one's lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy.

False belief that another person is in love with him/her. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

·         Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc., it is called Cotard syndrome.

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes he/she is financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about him/her (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

The period 1951–1981 is widely recognized as the phase of population explosion in India. This phase is characterized by:

  • Significant improvements after independence in medical facilities and food supply.

Demographic trap

  • This phenomenon refers to a period in which there is high fertility and birth rate and a declining death rate. The population grows exponentially in this stage and this growing population exceeds the national or regional carrying capacity. Countries in this stage are said to be caught in a demographic trap.
  • It is seen maximally in the early expanding stage (stage 2).

India is currently in stage-3 of the demographic cycle.

The year 1921 is called the year of the great divide in India. This is because, since 1921, the absolute number of people getting added to the population during each decade has been on the rise. This is the year in which India moved from stage 1 to stage 2 of the demographic cycle.

Stages of the demographic cycle include:

Stage 1

High stationary

·         High birth rates and high death rates render the population stationary

·         Narrow demographic gap

Stage 2

Early expanding

·         The death rate declines and the birth rate remains unchanged

·         The demographic gap starts increasing and becomes maximum

Stage 3

Late expanding

·         Death rate declines further and birth rate falls

·         India is in this stage

·         The demographic gap starts declining

Stage 4

Low stationary

·         Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

·         Narrow demographic gap

Stage 5

Declining

·         The population begins to decline as the birth rate is lower than the death rate

·         The demographic gap is negative

  • Dry powder inhalers scatter the drug into a fine powder that is dispersed by air turbulence on inhalation. DPls have been developed to deliver drugs such as insulin, but the dosing is inconsistent. Children below 7 years find it difficult to use a DPI.

Figure: Dry powder inhaler

  • Spacers reduce the velocity and size of particles entering the upper airways, enhancing drug delivery to the lower airways while minimizing oropharyngeal deposition. This results in less drug being swallowed and absorbed, limiting local side effects. Spacer devices are beneficial for children unable to use a pMDI alone and can also improve delivery for adults. They are especially recommended for children under 3 years of age when used with a face mask. A spacer device can be prescribed to decrease the incidence of propellant-mediated oropharyngeal adverse effects.

Figure: Spacer device

  • Nebulizers deliver much higher drug doses compared with pressurized metered-dose inhalers and are therefore particularly useful in the treatment of acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD, in patients with severe airway obstruction such as advanced COPD, in infants and small children who are unable to use other inhalation devices effectively, and for administering inhaled drugs like antibiotics that require relatively high doses.
  • Two types of nebulizers are available:

    i. Jet nebulizers that are driven by a stream of gas (air or oxygen)

    ii. Ultrasonic nebulizers that use a rapidly vibrating piezoelectric crystal and thus do not require a source of compressed gas.

 

Figure: Nebulizer

choices.title: Rickets
choices.correct_explanation:
• The clinical features are suggestive of Rickets, caused by the deficiency of vitamin D. This occurs due to poor dietary intake of vitamin D and also due to poor exposure to sunlight. The peak incidence is encountered in the age group 6 months to 2 years of age.
  • Features of Rickets:
    • Craniotabes (soft skull), frontal bossing, stunted growth, and craniosynostosis are clinical features of rickets.
    • General features include failure to thrive, listlessness, protruding abdomen, proximal muscle weakness, and fracture.
  • Head to toe-examination includes the following features:
    • Head examination would include craniotabes, frontal bossing, delayed fontanel closure, delayed dentition, and craniosynostosis.
    • Chest examination would reveal rachitic rosary, Harrison’s sulcus, and repeated respiratory infections and atelectasis.
    • Spinal deformities could include kyphosis, scoliosis, lordosis.
    • Limb examination and extremities may show windswept deformity, anterior bowing of tibia, coxa vara, and enlargement of wrists and ankles. Bowings of legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum) may be noted. These changes can be seen only in children of the weight-bearing age group/ toddlers.

Figure: Frontal bossing

Figure: Rachitic rosary

Radiological features of rickets:

  • Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.
  • Delayed appearance of the epiphysis
  • Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth plate is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.
  • Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.
  • Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis
  • Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices
  • In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

Figure: Fraying and cupping of the metaphysis

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

  • Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia
  • Wrist: especially the ulna
  • Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

Figure: Bowing of legs in rickets

Windswept deformity (combination of valgus deformity of one leg with varus deformity of the other leg) is seen in rickets. It is also seen in rheumatoid arthritis but characteristically seen in rickets.

Figure: Windswept deformity

Other deformities of extremities seen in rickets:

  • Enlargement of wrists and ankles
  • Valgus or varus deformities of limbs
  • Anterior bowing of the tibia and femur
  • Coxa vara

choices.title: Autonomy
choices.correct_explanation:
• Autonomy refers to a patient’s right to make decisions about his/her own care.
  • In this scenario:
    • The patient expresses pain and requests local anesthesia.
    • The nurse ignores the request and continues the procedure.

This disrespects the patient’s choice and consent, thus violating autonomy.

  • Why autonomy is violated:
    • Patients have the right to:
      • Accept or refuse treatment
      • Request pain relief
    • Ignoring their request = denial of self-determination

Other Options:

  • Option A. Beneficence (doing good): Not the primary issue here.
  • Option B. Non-maleficence (do no harm): Pain is caused, but the key issue is ignoring patient’s decision.
  • Option D. Justice (fairness): No issue of equality or resource distribution.
